issues.legal_issue: Notice to proposed defendants is not a statutory precondition to granting leave to institute a qualifying public-trust suit.
material_facts: The plaintiffs brought a representative suit seeking, among other relief, a scheme for a public charitable trust, and leave was required to institute it.
The court granted leave without notifying the proposed defendants.
The proposed defendants challenged the grant of leave on the ground that they had not been heard.
issues.conclusion: The court should normally, as a rule of caution, notify proposed defendants before granting leave unless doing so is impracticable or inconvenient. Notice is not a statutory requirement, however, and leave granted without notice does not make the suit invalid or non-maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, leave is required for a qualifying suit by interested persons unless all beneficiaries join. The court considered the purpose of preventing frivolous or harassing suits while avoiding delay or loss to a public trust, and held that notice is ordinarily desirable but not mandatory. Swami Parmatmanand Saraswati v. Ramji Tripathi and Charan Singh v. Darshan Singh were cited on the nature of the preliminary inquiry; T.N. Shanmugam v. Periyar Self Respect Propaganda Institution and various High Court decisions reflected differing views on notice. The court held that the Supreme Court cases cited did not decide whether notice was required.

predicates.qualifying_public_trust_suit: The plaintiffs bring a suit concerning a public charitable or religious trust seeking relief of the kind for which prior court permission is required.
predicates.leave_granted_without_notice: The court grants permission to institute the suit without first notifying the proposed defendants.

issues.definition: When a qualifying public-trust suit receives permission without prior notice to the proposed defendants, the absence of notice alone does not invalidate the suit.

issues.legal_issue: Prior court leave is a condition precedent to a qualifying public-trust suit when all beneficiaries do not join in instituting it.
material_facts: The plaintiffs instituted a representative suit concerning a public charitable trust without all beneficiaries joining as plaintiffs.
The plaintiffs applied for and obtained court leave to institute the suit.
issues.conclusion: Leave is a precondition to instituting a qualifying suit by interested persons unless all beneficiaries join; a suit instituted without the required leave is not maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 92(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits the Advocate-General, or two or more persons interested in the trust who have obtained the court’s leave, to institute a suit for the specified public-trust reliefs. The court relied on the language and purpose of the provision and cited Mahant Pragdasji Guru Bhagwandasji v. Patel Ishwarlalbhai Narsibhai and Charan Singh v. Darshan Singh on the special nature of a suit under section 92.

rule.if: qualifying_public_trust_suit and not all_beneficiaries_joined and not leave_obtained

predicates.qualifying_public_trust_suit: The plaintiffs bring a suit concerning a public charitable or religious trust seeking relief of the kind for which prior court permission is required.
predicates.all_beneficiaries_joined: Every beneficiary joins in instituting the suit.
predicates.leave_obtained: The plaintiffs obtain the court’s permission before instituting the suit.

issues.definition: A qualifying public-trust suit is not maintainable if all beneficiaries do not join and the plaintiffs have not obtained prior court permission.

issues.legal_issue: Proposed defendants may apply to revoke leave granted to institute a qualifying public-trust suit, and the application must be decided on its merits.
material_facts: The proposed defendants applied to revoke the leave, arguing in part that they had not been given an opportunity to be heard before it was granted.
The trial court dismissed the application as unnecessary because it regarded the grant of leave as administrative.
The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s order and directed the trial court to decide the revocation application on its merits and according to law.
issues.conclusion: The grant of leave does not defeat or seriously prejudice the proposed defendants’ rights because they may apply for revocation, which must be considered on its merits and according to law.
issues.legal_principle: The court held that the availability of an application to revoke leave protects proposed defendants from serious prejudice when leave has been granted without notice. Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs the leave requirement. Section 104(1)(ffa), which allows an appeal from refusal of leave, does not make notice obligatory before leave is granted because an appeal lies from refusal, not grant.

predicates.qualifying_public_trust_suit: The plaintiffs bring a suit concerning a public charitable or religious trust seeking relief of the kind for which prior court permission is required.
predicates.leave_granted: The court has granted permission to institute the suit.
predicates.proposed_defendants_seek_revocation: The proposed defendants apply to have the permission revoked.

issues.definition: When permission has been granted in a qualifying public-trust suit and the proposed defendants seek revocation, their application is considered on its merits.
